official_questions.rule: Borrowings: USA - FR, judicial review, impeachment; UK - parliamentary system, rule of law; Ireland - DPSP; Australia - Concurrent List, joint sitting; Canada - residuary with Centre.

official_questions.stem: From which Constitution the concept of concurrent list has borrowed:
official_questions.core_fact: The Concurrent List, freedom of trade and commerce and joint sitting of the two Houses were borrowed from the Australian Constitution.

statements.t: The concept of the Concurrent List was borrowed from the Constitution of Australia.

official_questions.rule: Australia: Concurrent List, trade & commerce, joint sitting; Canada: federation with strong Centre, residuary powers with Centre.

official_questions.stem: The Constitution of India adopted the Federal System from the Act of:
official_questions.core_fact: The federal scheme, Governor's office, judiciary, PSCs, emergency provisions and administrative details were largely drawn from the Government of India Act 1935.

statements.t: The Constitution of India adopted the federal system from the Government of India Act of 1935.

official_questions.rule: GoI Act 1935 = largest single source (federal scheme, Governor, emergency, PSCs).

official_questions.stem: When was the National Anthem officially adopted by the Constituent assembly as the Indian National anthem.
official_questions.core_fact: On 24 January 1950 (last session) the Constituent Assembly adopted 'Jana Gana Mana' as the national anthem and 'Vande Mataram' as national song, and elected Rajendra Prasad President.

statements.t: The National Anthem was officially adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 24 January 1950.

official_questions.rule: 22 July 1947 national flag; 26 Nov 1949 Constitution adopted; 24 Jan 1950 anthem, song, Prasad elected; 26 Jan 1950 commencement.

official_questions.stem: Which of the following is not a fundamental right?
official_questions.core_fact: The right to work is a Directive Principle (Art. 41: right to work, education and public assistance), not a Fundamental Right; equality (14-18), freedom (19-22) and freedom of religion (25-28) are FRs.

statements.t: The right to work is not a Fundamental Right (it is a Directive Principle under Article 41).

official_questions.rule: Economic rights (work, living wage, education <6) are DPSPs; FRs are six groups (14-18, 19-22, 23-24, 25-28, 29-30, 32).

official_questions.stem: Preamble is a part of the Constitution and relates to its basic structure Frame work was held in
official_questions.key: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala.
official_questions.core_fact: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (1973, 13 judges) held the Preamble to be part of the Constitution, amendable under Art. 368 without destroying the basic structure (overruling Berubari 1960 on this point); LIC of India (1995) reaffirmed.

statements.t: The Preamble was held to be part of the Constitution and related to its basic structure in Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala.

official_questions.rule: Berubari 1960: Preamble not part; Kesavananda 1973: part + basic structure; LIC 1995: part of Constitution.

official_questions.stem: The chief source of political power in India is
official_questions.core_fact: The Preamble opens 'We, the people of India ... do hereby adopt, enact and give to ourselves this Constitution' - the people are the ultimate source of political power; organs derive authority from the Constitution.

statements.t: The chief source of political power in India is the people.

official_questions.rule: Source of authority = people; nature of State = sovereign socialist secular democratic republic; date of adoption = 26 Nov 1949.

official_questions.stem: A law is void only to the extent of inconsistency with fundamental rights and if that part is severable, the law remains valid and alive which is consistent with fundamental rights. This doctrine is
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 13 makes a law void 'to the extent of' inconsistency with FRs; only the offending severable part is struck down (A.K. Gopalan 1950; R.M.D.C. v UoI 1957) - doctrine of severability.

statements.t: A law void only to the extent of inconsistency with fundamental rights, with the severable consistent part remaining valid, reflects the doctrine of severability.

official_questions.rule: Art. 13 doctrines: severability (cut off bad part), eclipse (pre-Constitution law dormant), waiver (FRs cannot be waived).

official_questions.stem: "Right to life" does not include "right to die". It has been held in case of
official_questions.key: Chenna Jagadeswar v. State of A.P.
official_questions.core_fact: In Chenna Jagadeeswar v State of AP (1988) the AP High Court held that Art. 21 does not include a right to die and upheld IPC s.309; the SC later held the same in Gian Kaur (1996), overruling P. Rathinam (1994).

statements.t: 'Right to life does not include right to die' was held in Chenna Jagadeeswar v State of AP.

official_questions.rule: Right to die: Bhatia (Del HC 1985) yes; Chenna Jagadeeswar (AP HC 1988) no; Rathinam (SC 1994) yes; Gian Kaur (SC 1996) no; Common Cause (2018) passive euthanasia allowed.
official_questions.key_note: Key kept. The draft analysis wrongly keyed Gian Kaur; APPSC's key is Chenna Jagadeeswar (AP HC 1988), which held the same.

official_questions.stem: Article 23 of the Indian Constitution prohibits
official_questions.key: traffic in human beings and forced labour.
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 23 prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and other similar forms of forced labour; the State may impose compulsory service for public purposes without discrimination. Art. 24 bans child labour in hazardous employment below 14.

statements.t: Article 23 of the Constitution prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour.
statements.d: traffic in human beings and forced labour

official_questions.rule: Art. 17 untouchability; Art. 23 trafficking & forced labour; Art. 24 child labour (<14, hazardous).

official_questions.stem: Compelling to incriminate himself in a case is
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 20(3): no person accused of an offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself (protection against self-incrimination; Selvi v State of Karnataka 2010 on narco tests). Art. 20(1) ex post facto, 20(2) double jeopardy.

statements.t: Compelling an accused to incriminate himself in a case is self-incrimination, prohibited by Article 20(3).

official_questions.rule: Art. 20: (1) no ex post facto, (2) no double jeopardy, (3) no self-incrimination.

official_questions.stem: What are the provisions of the directive principles under Article 45 of our constitution?
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 45 (as substituted by the 86th Amendment 2002): the State shall endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete six years. Original Art. 45: free and compulsory education until 14 within 10 years (now Art. 21A).

statements.t: Article 45 directs the State to endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of six years.

official_questions.rule: 86th Amendment 2002: Art. 21A (6-14 education FR), Art. 45 (ECCE <6), Art. 51A(k) (parents' duty).
official_questions.key_note: Deleted by APPSC (no key). Statement verified from the constitutional text (basis fact).

official_questions.stem: Out of the following terms, which one has not been used in the Preamble of the Indian Constitution ?
official_questions.core_fact: The Preamble secures Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty (of thought, expression...), Equality (of status and opportunity) and Fraternity; the word 'Freedom' is not used.

statements.t: The term 'Liberty' has not been used in the Preamble.

official_questions.stem: Articles 5 – 11 of the Indian Constitution deals with
official_questions.core_fact: Articles 5-11 (Part II) deal with citizenship; Part I (Arts 1-4) Union and its territory; Part III (Arts 12-35) Fundamental Rights; Part IVA (Art. 51A) Fundamental Duties.

official_questions.stem: “...all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practice and propagate religion” is mentioned in which Article ?
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 25(1): all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality, health.

statements.t: The freedom of conscience and right to profess, practise and propagate religion is in Article 22.
The freedom of conscience and right to profess, practise and propagate religion is in Article 26.

official_questions.stem: Which Article of the Indian Constitution contains provision for “Promotion of Educational and Economic Interests of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other Weaker Sections” ?
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 46 (DPSP): State shall promote with special care the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections, especially SCs and STs.

statements.t: The provision for promotion of educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections is in Article 44.
The provision for promotion of educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections is in Article 32.

The provision for promotion of educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections is in Article 46.

official_questions.stem: The Preamble of Indian Constitution declares India as
official_questions.core_fact: The Preamble declares India a Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic; it uses none of 'unitary', 'federal' or 'quasi-federal' (Art. 1: 'Union of States').

statements.t: The Preamble declares India as Unitary State.
statements.fact: Preamble: Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic.

statements.fact: The word 'federal' is not used anywhere in the Constitution.

statements.t: The Preamble declares India as Quasi-federal State.
statements.fact: 'Quasi-federal' is Wheare's scholarly label, not the Preamble's.

statements.t: The Preamble declares India as None of the above.

official_questions.rule: Preamble declares SSSDR; 'federal' never used; Art. 1 'Union of States'.

official_questions.stem: According to which Article of the Indian Constitution, ‘No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once’ ?
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 20(2): no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once (double jeopardy); 20(1) ex post facto; 20(3) self-incrimination.

statements.t: 'No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once' is in Article 19.
statements.fact: Art. 19 lists freedoms of speech, assembly etc.

statements.t: 'No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once' is in Article 20.
'No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once' is in Article 21.
statements.fact: Art. 21 protects life and personal liberty.

statements.t: 'No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once' is in Article 22.

official_questions.rule: Art. 20: (1) ex post facto, (2) double jeopardy, (3) self-incrimination; not suspendable in emergency (44th Am.).

official_questions.stem:
Which of the following is/are among the fundamental duties of citizens in the Indian Constitution ?
(i) To uphold and protect the Sovereignty, Unity and Integrity of India.
(ii) To protect the weaker sections from social injustice.
(iii) To value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture.
(iv) To promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India.
Select the correct answer from the given code :
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 51A lists (c) uphold sovereignty, unity and integrity; (e) promote harmony and common brotherhood; (f) value and preserve composite culture. Protecting weaker sections from social injustice is the DPSP Art. 46.

statements.t: To uphold and protect the Sovereignty, Unity and Integrity of India is a fundamental duty.
To protect the weaker sections from social injustice is a fundamental duty.
statements.d: protect the weaker sections from social injustice
statements.fact: Protecting weaker sections from social injustice is a Directive Principle (Art. 46), not a citizen's duty.

statements.t: To value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture is a fundamental duty.
To promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India is a fundamental duty.

official_questions.rule: Art. 51A addresses citizens; 'protect weaker sections' (Art. 46) addresses the State.

official_questions.stem: By which of the following Acts, the Governor General of Bengal was designated as the Governor General of India ?
official_questions.core_fact: The Charter Act 1833 designated the Governor-General of Bengal as the Governor-General of India (Lord William Bentinck first), with all civil and military powers - the final step towards centralisation. The GoI Act 1858 made him Viceroy.

statements.t: The Governor-General of Bengal was designated as the Governor-General of India by the Charter Act of 1853.
statements.fact: The 1833 Charter Act made the GG of Bengal GG of India.

statements.t: The Governor-General of Bengal was designated as the Governor-General of India by the Charter Act of 1793.
statements.fact: The 1833 Charter Act made the GG of Bengal GG of India.

statements.t: The Governor-General of Bengal was designated as the Governor-General of India by the Charter Act of 1833.
The Governor-General of Bengal was designated as the Governor-General of India by the Government of India Act 1858.

statements.fact: 1858 made the GG also 'Viceroy'; the 'GG of India' title came in 1833.

official_questions.stem: The 11th Fundamental Duty was added by which Constitutional Amendment Act ?
official_questions.core_fact: The 86th Amendment Act 2002 added Art. 51A(k) - duty of a parent/guardian to provide opportunities for education to a child between 6 and 14 - along with Art. 21A and the new Art. 45.

statements.t: The 11th Fundamental Duty was added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2001.

statements.t: The 11th Fundamental Duty was added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002.
The 11th Fundamental Duty was added by the 96th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2001.

official_questions.rule: 86th Amd 2002: Art. 21A + new 45 + 51A(k); RTE Act 2009 in force 1 Apr 2010.

The 1861 Act introduced portfolio system and ordinances.

official_questions.stem: Which of the following objectives is not embodied in the Preamble to the Constitution of India ?
official_questions.core_fact: The Preamble secures JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and opportunity. 'Political' qualifies justice, not liberty.

statements.t: Political Liberty is an objective embodied in the Preamble to the Constitution of India.

Liberty of Belief is an objective embodied in the Preamble to the Constitution of India.
Liberty of Expression is an objective embodied in the Preamble to the Constitution of India.

List - A / List - B
a. Art. 137 - i. Restoring Fundamental Rights by Supreme Court by issuing writs.

c. Art. 13 - iii. The High Courts also have the power to issue Writs for protecting Fundamental Rights.
d. Art. 32 - iv. Supreme Court can declare the concerned law as unconstitutional.

statements.t: Article 137 gives the Supreme Court power to review any judgment or order made by it.

official_questions.stem:
Assertion (A) : Right to Property is made a legal right under Article 300-A in Part XII of the Constitution.
Reason (R) : 44th Amendment Act of 1978 eliminated the Right to Property from the list of Fundamental Rights.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
official_questions.key: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
official_questions.core_fact: The 44th Amendment (1978) deleted Arts 19(1)(f) and 31 from Part III and inserted Art. 300A (Part XII, Chapter IV): 'No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law' - a constitutional/legal right.

statements.t: Right to Property is made a legal right under Article 300-A in Part XII of the Constitution.
The 44th Amendment Act of 1978 eliminated the Right to Property from the list of Fundamental Rights.
R explains A: removal from the FR list by the 44th Amendment is why property became a legal right under Art. 300A.

official_questions.rule: Property: FR until 1978 -> legal/constitutional right (Art. 300A); 31A, 31B, 31C survive.

official_questions.stem:
Assertion (A) : Directive Principles of State Policy are not capable of being independently enforced in a Court of Law.
Reason (R) : They act as guide post for legislation.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
official_questions.key: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 37: DPSPs shall not be enforceable by any court but are fundamental in governance and the State shall apply them in making laws. They are non-justiciable because Art. 37 says so (and resources may be lacking), not because they guide legislation.

statements.t: Directive Principles of State Policy are not capable of being independently enforced in a court of law.
statements.d: not capable of being independently enforced

statements.t: They act as guideposts for legislation.
R explains A: acting as guideposts for legislation is why DPSPs are not enforceable.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked
statements.fact: Both true; non-justiciability flows from Art. 37's express bar, not from their role as guides.

official_questions.rule: Art. 37 = non-justiciable + fundamental in governance; courts use DPSPs to interpret FRs (harmonious construction).
official_questions.key_note: APPSC's final key changed the answer from option 1 to option 2 (R not the correct explanation). Kept.

official_questions.stem:
Are the statements given below in the Indian Constitution ?
Statement (A) : Ownership and control of the material resources of the community are so distributed as best to subserve the common good.
Statement (B) : Operation of the economic system does not result in the concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment.
options: Both Statements (A) and (B) are not there
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 39(b): ownership and control of material resources of the community so distributed as best to subserve the common good; Art. 39(c): operation of the economic system not to result in concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment. (Property Owners Assn v State of Maharashtra, Nov 2024: not all private property is 'material resources of the community').

statements.t: The Constitution provides that ownership and control of the material resources of the community are so distributed as best to subserve the common good.
The Constitution provides that the operation of the economic system does not result in the concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment.

official_questions.rule: Art. 39(b)/(c) protected by Art. 31C (25th Amd 1971); 2024 nine-judge ruling narrowed 'material resources'.

official_questions.stem:

a. Free Legal Aid
b. Maternity Relief
c. Living Wage
d. Safeguarding of Forests
e. Protection of Monuments
options: a, b, c, d and e
official_questions.key: a, b, c, d and e
official_questions.core_fact: Free legal aid - Art. 39A (42nd Amd); just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief - Art. 42; living wage - Art. 43; protection of environment, forests and wildlife - Art. 48A (42nd Amd); protection of monuments - Art. 49.

statements.t: Directive Principles contain free legal aid.
Directive Principles contain maternity relief.
Directive Principles contain living wage.
Directive Principles contain safeguarding of forests.
Directive Principles contain protection of monuments.

official_questions.rule: 42nd Amd added 39(f), 39A, 43A, 48A; 44th added 38(2); 86th changed 45; 97th added 43B.

official_questions.stem:
Statement (A) : There is no fundamental right to marry.
Statement (B) : Right to travel abroad comes under the purview of Fundamental Rights.
options: Statement (A) is right and Statement (B) is wrong
Statement (A) is wrong and Statement (B) is right
official_questions.core_fact: Right to travel abroad is part of personal liberty under Art 21 (Satwant Singh Sawhney 1967; Maneka Gandhi 1978). APPSC's key treats marriage as not an independent enumerated fundamental right.

Right to travel abroad comes under the purview of Fundamental Rights.

official_questions.rule: Art 21 reads in travel abroad (Maneka); marriage-choice is protected (Shafin Jahan) but a standalone right to marry was denied (Supriyo 2023) – read the wording.

official_questions.stem: Which of the following is not a Fundamental Duty as mentioned in the Constitution ?
options: To safeguard public property and to abjure violence
To value and preserve the rich heritage of the country's composite culture
To protect the elderly, differently abled and children
To promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood

statements.t: 'To safeguard public property and to abjure violence' is a Fundamental Duty in Article 51A.

statements.t: 'To value and preserve the rich heritage of the country's composite culture' is a Fundamental Duty in Article 51A.

Assertion (A) : The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act (1976) is known as 'Mini-Constitution'.

Which of the following statements are true regarding 97th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2011 ?
A. Gave Constitutional status and protection to Co-operative Societies.
B. Made the right to form Co-operative Societies a Fundamental Right under Article 19.

official_questions.core_fact: The 97th Amendment (2011, in force 15 Feb 2012) gave constitutional status to co-operative societies: added 'or co-operative societies' to Art. 19(1)(c), inserted DPSP Art. 43B, and added Part IXB (Arts 243ZH-243ZT). The 97th Amendment added a new Part X-B to the Constitution.
statements.fact: The 97th Amendment added Part IXB (The Co-operative Societies), after Part IXA (Municipalities).

statements.t: The 97th Amendment added a new Directive Principle under Article 43-B.

official_questions.rule: Part numbering: IX (73rd), IXA (74th), IXB (97th); Part X = Scheduled & Tribal areas.
official_questions.key_note: Time note: Part IXB was partly struck down (State co-operatives) in UoI v Rajendra N. Shah (2021); statements describe the Amendment as enacted.
